analysis.one_liner: Caps Medicare drug cost-sharing for seniors at the plan's net price after manufacturer discounts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or floor vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change Medicare's prescription drug benefit so that when seniors pick up a covered drug, their copay or coinsurance is capped at the plan's negotiated price minus any manufacturer price concessions — the 'net price' the plan actually keeps. Today, Part D cost-sharing is often based on a higher gross price even after pharmacy-price concessions have reduced what the plan really pays, so seniors can pay more than the plan's real cost. Plans that violate the cap would face civil money penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D enrollees, roughly tens of millions of seniors and disabled beneficiaries. Anyone whose cost-sharing today is calculated on a price higher than what the plan actually receives after manufacturer concessions would see their out-of-pocket costs drop or stay capped at the plan's true net price. Low-income beneficiaries would get a matching cap on their copayments.

how_it_helps.text: Beginning in plan year 2026, cost-sharing (after the annual deductible) for a covered Part D drug could not exceed the drug's negotiated price net of manufacturer-provided price concessions, as reported in the plan's Detailed DIR Report.
Plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage drug plans that violate the cap would be subject to civil monetary penalties, with the Secretary of Health and Human Services setting the amount.
Copayments for low-income subsidy beneficiaries would be capped at the same net-price amount for plan year 2026 and after.

analysis.who_pays: Part D plan sponsors — insurance companies and Medicare Advantage plans that administer the drug benefit — would lose the spread between the gross price on which cost-sharing is based and the net price they actually keep after manufacturer concessions. Some of that could be recovered by adjusting premiums or plan design, but the immediate cost of the rule falls on the plans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug plan insurers and Medicare Advantage plans

drawbacks.text: Plans that lose the cost-sharing spread would face pressure to raise premiums or trim benefits to offset it, so some savings to seniors at the pharmacy counter could be partly offset in premiums.

The bill ties the cap to the Detailed DIR Report figures, which reflect past-year concessions, so reported net prices may not always match the plan's real-time economics, creating compliance and measurement questions for plans and regulators.
The penalty for violations is left to the Secretary's discretion with no specified amount, so enforcement strength is uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: seniors' out-of-pocket costs at the pharmacy are capped at the plan's actual net price, and plans give up a billing spread that beneficiaries often never see. The offset risk — plans raising premiums or narrowing benefits — is real but modest, and the low-income copay cap plus civil penalties give the rule teeth. The main weakness is not design but inaction: the bill never received a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2023 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Casey (D-PA) introduced the bill on July 20, 2023, for himself and Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX).
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; that was the bill's last action.
It received one cosponsor, a Republican, and the Finance Committee never scheduled a hearing or markup before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Part D plan sponsors and pharmacy-benefit intermediaries keep the billing spread between gross and net prices, and Medicare beneficiaries continue to pay cost-sharing that can exceed the plan's real net cost of a drug.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug plan insurers keep the billing spread

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat sponsoring with a top Texas Republican cosponsor — but with only one cosponsor beyond Sen. Casey, there was never enough backing to move it through committee.

industries.industry: Part D plan sponsors (insurers and Medicare Advantage plans)
industries.note: Today, beneficiary cost-sharing can be based on a gross price even after manufacturer concessions reduce what the plan actually keeps. The bill would cap what seniors pay at the plan's net price, taking away that spread from the plans.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and pharmacy-price concession intermediaries
industries.note: The bill does not ban manufacturer price concessions, which flow through PBM intermediaries; it only requires that the concessions be passed through to what beneficiaries pay. The concession system itself stays intact, but the plans and intermediaries lose the ability to charge seniors on the pre-concession price.

Their existing price concessions continue, but beneficiaries' lower out-of-pocket costs could improve adherence and prescription volume; the bill imposes no new direct price controls on manufacturers.
